The server room hummed at three in the morning, and Amber sat on an overturned milk crate with her laptop balanced on her knees. Two states away, in a converted garage office, Katherine was looking at the same dataset on her own screen. They had been trading voice notes since midnight.

For eight months they had been the only two independent researchers digging into the same procurement scandal — Amber working her sources inside the state comptroller's office, Katherine working hers among the contractors. They'd shared tips freely. They'd celebrated each other's small breaks. There was an understanding, mostly unspoken, that when they were ready, they would publish a joint piece and split the byline.

Then the leak landed in both their inboxes within the same hour. The same documents. A complete paper trail. Either of them could file it solo by morning and own the story.

Amber rubbed her eyes. The thing about a joint byline was that it diluted the win. A reporter who broke this alone would be on every cable show by Tuesday. A reporter who shared it would be on a panel, maybe, in three weeks. They both knew this. Neither had said it.

"You still there?" Katherine's voice came through the laptop speaker, scratchy.

"Still here."

"I keep thinking," Katherine said slowly, "about what happens if we both rush it. Two competing versions of the same story hit the wire within an hour of each other. Editors get nervous. Sources get spooked. The piece looks fragmented. Half the impact, for both of us."

"I know."

"And if one of us holds and the other doesn't —" Katherine stopped. "I don't want to say it like that."

"I know what you mean."

There was a long quiet. Amber listened to the hum of the cooling fans and thought about the trust they'd built, and about the agent who'd called her last week saying a book deal was very possible if she had a signature scoop. Katherine had probably gotten a similar call. They didn't talk about those calls.

Either of them could hit send on a solo draft tonight. Or either could wait until morning and work the joint piece, trusting that the other would do the same. There was no way to verify the other's choice in advance. By the time anyone knew anything, it would already be done.

Filing the joint piece by morning, holding back the solo version — that was what they were quietly calling Decision A. Pushing her own draft out tonight, ahead of any coordination — Decision B.

Amber's cursor hovered. Through the speaker she could hear Katherine breathing, the faint click of a keyboard, then silence again.

"I'm going to go think for a minute," Katherine said.

"Yeah," Amber said. "Me too."

The call ended. The cursor blinked.

The text from Jamil came through at 11:47 p.m., while Hana was still at her kitchen table with cold tea and a binder full of grievance forms.

*They offered me the same thing they offered you, I'd bet. Talk tomorrow before the 9 a.m.?*

She read it twice. Then a third time, looking for the thing underneath the words.

For seven months, Local 414 and Local 622 had bargained as a bloc. Two plants, two presidents, one front. The company had tried every wedge — staggered meetings, "informational" memos slipped under different doors, a friendly VP who happened to call Jamil's cell on a Sunday. Hana and Jamil had laughed about it on their weekly Zoom. *They think we don't talk.* They did talk. They talked all the time.

Then, yesterday, the company's lead negotiator had taken Hana into a side room and laid out a number — a real number, on paper, with a signature line — that would make 622's people whole on pensions, on shift differentials, on the back-pay claims she'd been fighting since before her father died. The number was good. It was so good her stomach turned. The catch was small and quiet: sign now, alone, before the joint session resumed. The offer would not be repeated, and it would not be made if 414 settled first under similar terms.

She hadn't said yes. She hadn't said no. She'd said she needed to sleep on it, and the negotiator had smiled like a man who knew how sleep went.

Now, at midnight, Jamil's text sat on her screen.

She wanted to believe the obvious thing — that he was reaching out for the same reason she would have, to confirm the squeeze, to lock arms again before morning. He'd been her ally since the first organizing drive. He'd brought soup to her house when her father was in hospice. She trusted him. She did.

And yet.

If he'd already signed, a late-night text was exactly the move that would keep her steady, keep her looking forward, keep her at the joint table tomorrow as cover while his local quietly walked away with the prize. She hated that the thought had even formed. She hated more that she couldn't unform it. The negotiator had been too smooth, too rehearsed; he'd run this play before, on someone, somewhere, and it had worked.

She thought about her members. The forklift drivers. The single mom on second shift who'd cornered her in the parking lot last week and asked, without quite asking, whether something was finally going to happen. Hana had promised her a real answer soon. She had not promised solidarity in the abstract; she had promised her *something*. The number on the paper was something. Holding the line was a bet that Jamil was holding it too.

She typed: *Yeah. 7:30, my place.* Deleted it. Typed it again. Sent it.

Then she sat with the binder and the cold tea and the two paths she'd been turning over since yesterday afternoon — what she'd started, in her own head, to call Decision A, the one where she walked into the 9 a.m. session tomorrow with the side offer untouched in her bag and her shoulder against Jamil's, and Decision B, the one where she signed the page in the side room before the session began and let her people have the thing she could actually hand them.

The clock rolled past one. Jamil hadn't replied yet about 7:30. She watched the three dots appear, vanish, appear again.

They'd been collaborators for eleven years, since their postdoc days, and their two labs — Christopher's at the marine station up the coast, Mason's at the inland university — had spent the last three running parallel arms of a sediment-microbiome study. The funder had just informed them, gently but unmistakably, that continued support hinged on a "consolidated dataset" submitted by each PI individually. Each lab would file its own package. The reviewers would compare.

Here was the wrinkle, the thing that made Christopher's stomach knot as he drove the two hours to meet Mason at the halfway diner: the program officer had let slip that whichever lab presented the "more complete" picture would likely anchor the next phase. The other would become a subcontractor, or fold into the anchor's program, or simply lose its line.

Mason was already in the back booth when Christopher arrived, stirring coffee he wasn't drinking.

"You saw the language," Mason said.

"I saw it."

They both knew what they had. Christopher's team had clean isotope work but thin sequencing depth. Mason's had the sequencing — gorgeous, deep, expensive sequencing — but their isotope runs had been compromised by a calibration issue last spring. Pooled, the two datasets told a story neither could tell alone, and a beautiful one. Submitted together as a unified package, both labs would clearly survive; the reviewers would see two PIs who had simply done one excellent project in two places.

But the submissions were independent. And if one of them quietly held back the strongest of their unique data — kept the crown jewels for their own filing while letting the other contribute everything they had — the holder would look like the indispensable one. The anchor. The other would look like the tributary.

Neither of them said this out loud. They didn't have to. They had spent a decade reading each other's silences in conference rooms.

"I trust you," Mason said finally.

"I trust you too." Christopher meant it. He also knew Mason was about to lose his second postdoc to a hiring freeze if the inland line didn't get renewed at full strength. He knew because Mason had told him, last month, drunk on bad wine at a workshop in Portugal.

And Mason knew that Christopher's marine station was hanging on by a thread that the university provost had been openly fingering for two years.

There was no enforcement mechanism. They would each prepare their packages over the weekend, in their own offices, with their own teams. They would each upload on Monday by noon. There would be no way to verify, after the fact, what the other had chosen to include or withhold — the funder's review was confidential, and reviewers wouldn't ever tell them which lab had submitted what. Whatever happened in those two offices on Saturday and Sunday would simply happen.

Christopher turned his coffee cup. "We submit the joint package. Everything we have. Both files identical on the shared sections."

"Yes," Mason said. "That's what I want too."

They looked at each other across the table, and Christopher felt the specific loneliness of knowing his friend was sincere right now, in this booth, and that sincerity in this booth was not the same thing as what each of them would actually type into the upload portal alone in their offices Sunday night. He could feel Mason calculating the same thing in reverse. Each of them was now imagining the other imagining them.

The waitress refilled their cups.

What they were each weighing, though neither would name it: go home and assemble the full unified package as agreed, every strong piece of unique evidence shared into the joint submission — call that Decision A — or quietly hold back the irreplaceable thread that only their lab possessed, file a package that subtly outshone the other's, and hope the friendship survived a result that the friend would never be able to prove was engineered. Decision B.

Christopher drove home in the dark thinking about his postdocs, about Mason's postdocs, about the eleven years, about Monday at noon.

"They're good at this," Ben said finally. "Whoever wrote their playbook."

"They've done it before."

"Probably to people who used to be friends."

If they walked into Monday's meeting aligned, refusing the side conversations, presenting only the joint terms — they'd get the clean deal. They'd both end up with less than the public terms had promised, and they'd have spent their friendship to get there.

"We could just agree," Ben said. "Right now. Nothing on the side. We go in together Monday."

Helio had been clear about the timeline without ever stating it. That was part of the playbook too.

Maya set down her cup. "I should go home."

"Yeah."

They hugged at the door, the way they always did, and she walked out into the cold not knowing what he would do, and not entirely sure, yet, what she would.

Both of them sat on grain estates in Campania the size of small kingdoms. Both had clients in every quarter who would remember, for a generation, who fed them in the dry year. The plan was simple in shape: each would send riders south tonight, and at dawn the gates of his granaries would be thrown wide, and wheat would flow into the city at the old price, the just price, the price that ruined a man and bought him the love of Rome forever.

A runner in his household livery stood now in the doorway, waiting for the sealed orders to take to the estate steward. Gaius had not yet pressed the ring into the wax.

He kept thinking of his daughter's dowry. Of the loan against the Sabine villa that came due in autumn. Of his second son, who would stand for the quaestorship next year and would need silver, much silver, to do it properly. To open the bins fully — every bin, the seed-stock, the reserves his grandfather had laid in against war years — was to walk out of this season a poor man wearing a garland. He could survive that, if Servius walked out beside him. They would rise together; the Memmii and the Rufini would be names spoken in the same breath in every insula for thirty years.

But.

If Servius, sitting in his own study across the city tonight, was thinking the same things Gaius was thinking — about his own daughter, his own loans, his own sons — and quietly decided to release only a portion, only what was decent, only what a careful man would risk — then Gaius would be the one ruined. Servius would still be praised; the city would still half-eat; and Gaius alone would emerge a pauper for the gesture. The thought was sour as old wine. And the inverse glittered no less brightly: if Gaius held a portion back while Servius emptied his stores, Gaius would keep his villa, keep his son's career, and still bask in the reflected gratitude of a fed city.

He trusted Servius. He had trusted Servius since they were boys throwing knucklebones in the Subura. That was not in question.

What was in question was whether Servius, alone in his own room with his own lamp, was at this moment trusting him back enough to do the thing that left him most exposed.

Gaius set down the tablet and picked up another, blank. Two sets of orders, then. He could write either. The runner shifted his weight. The instructions to the steward would either be the open-handed ones — every bin, every measure, the oath kept in full — or the careful ones, the ones a prudent paterfamilias might draft, releasing enough to be seen and remembered, holding enough to weather the year.

What he and Servius had each privately begun calling, in their own thoughts, Decision A and Decision B.

Across the city, in a study Gaius could not see, another lamp was burning low, and another runner was waiting at another door.

Marcus Caelius and Titus Naevius had run amphorae of Baetican oil up the Rhône for nine years together, splitting the cost of the river-boats and the bribes to the customs officers at Arelate. This year, an unexpected glut had crashed the price in Lugdunum. Each man had a warehouse there full of jars he could not sell at cost.

They had agreed, in a long evening over thin Gallic wine, to hold the line: neither would sell below a floor price for forty days, allowing the local market to absorb the excess and prices to recover. Together they were the largest suppliers in the city. Together their restraint would work.

But each man also knew that if he alone broke the agreement quietly — sold his stock fast, at a discount, before word spread — he would clear his warehouse while his partner held idle inventory that would only depreciate further. The early seller would recover his capital and ride south for the winter. The one who held the line would find his oil rancid and his loans called.

And if both raced to dump? Marcus had seen this happen in Massalia six years back to two olive merchants who had tried the same trick on each other. They had broken the floor on the same morning. Buyers, smelling the panic, had crushed both prices to nothing. One man hanged himself. The other took ship for Africa and was not heard from again.

The two of them stood now on the wooden dock above the slow brown river, watching slaves roll empty amphorae down the planks. The forty days began at dawn.

"You know I am good for it," Titus said.

"I know it." Marcus did know it. He also knew that Titus's daughter was to be married in spring, and the dowry was not yet whole.

"And you?"

"I am good for it."

They clasped forearms. Each man would return to his own warehouse, his own foreman, his own ledger, and by tomorrow each would have given the order — either to keep the jars sealed and the prices firm, what they had been calling Decision A, or to start moving stock quietly through the back-alley brokers, Decision B. Neither would learn what the other had done until the market reports came out of Lugdunum a week hence.

Marcus walked back along the riverbank alone, listening to the gulls.

The flour shortage hit small bakeries first. By the third week of February, Renata Cosma had stopped answering calls from her wholesale customers and was mixing rye into everything she could to stretch what was left in her storeroom. She drove out to a diner in Rensselaer to meet Theo Park, who ran a bakery twenty minutes from hers and who had, six years earlier, lent her his proofing cabinet for an entire summer when hers died in the middle of wedding season.

Theo arrived with bags under his eyes. They ordered coffee and skipped the menus.

"I found a guy," Theo said.

"Pennsylvania?"

"Upstate. Mennonite mill, off the books. He has enough to keep one of us going through April. Maybe both of us, stretched thin."

The math sat between them like a wet rag. The mill owner had already told Theo he wanted a single buyer — a clean handshake, one name on the invoice. If Renata and Theo split the order, they'd each get enough to keep their ovens warm but not enough to fulfill the wholesale contracts that paid their leases. If one of them took it all, that one would survive the spring intact. The other would go dark on bread for at least a month and likely lose the café accounts that had taken years to build.

They had agreed to think it over separately. No texts, no nudges. Each of them would call the mill on Friday morning. The mill would honor whichever request came in with full payment first. If two arrived, the deal collapsed entirely — the old man had been clear: he didn't want to mediate.

Renata stirred her coffee and didn't look up. "If we both go for it ourselves, we both lose him."

"I know."

"And if we split it, we both come out of this scratched up but breathing."

"I know that too."

She did know what she was supposed to do. Theo had stood up at her father's funeral and read the Lord's Prayer in Romanian, badly, because no one else there could. He'd covered her Saturday market for three weeks running when her mother was dying. None of that was nothing.

But she also knew her landlord had sent a second notice. And that Theo's wife had just gotten a hospital job with benefits, and Theo's family would not, in the strictest sense, be on the street if his ovens went cold.

She drove home thinking about the call she'd place Friday morning — about whether she'd ask the mill to split the order, which they were quietly calling Decision A, or whether she'd ask for the whole shipment in her own name, Decision B, and let the chips fall.
